snapshots.name: Monnica
snapshots.body: Augustine's mother, a devout Christian whose prayers and tears run through the narrative from his boyhood to her death at Ostia, narrated at length in Book 9 as the book's most sustained portrait of grief and consolation. Named once, in the closing lines of Book 9's memorial to her; everywhere else she is "my mother."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alypius
snapshots.body: Augustine's closest friend from Thagaste, a fellow student and later a legal officer of notable integrity, who follows him through Manichaeism, Milan, and conversion, and is baptized alongside him. His own struggle with an addiction to the gladiatorial games is narrated at length in Book 6.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nebridius
snapshots.body: A friend from Carthage who leaves his family estate to join Augustine and Alypius in Milan, sharing their restless search for truth and wisdom; he recurs across Books 4, 6, 7, and 9 as a fellow seeker rather than a settled believer.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ambrose
snapshots.body: Bishop of Milan, whose sermons on the figurative interpretation of Scripture free Augustine from his Manichaean objections to the Old Testament and set him on the path to conversion; also shown defending Milan's church against imperial pressure in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Patricius
snapshots.body: Augustine's father, a citizen of Thagaste of modest means and, for most of his life, no religion; he is baptized shortly before his death, recounted briefly in Book 9. Named twice, both in Book 9's memorial passage; elsewhere he is "my father."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adeodatus
snapshots.body: Augustine's son, born to him in his youth by an unnamed mistress; present at the Cassiacum retreat before Augustine's baptism and baptized alongside him and Alypius.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Simplicianus
snapshots.body: An elderly priest in Milan, spiritual father to Ambrose, whom Augustine consults about Platonist philosophy; his account of the rhetorician Victorinus's conversion, in Book 8, becomes the example that shames Augustine into confronting his own hesitation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Victorinus
snapshots.body: A famous Roman rhetorician and translator of Platonist texts whose late-life conversion to Christianity, publicly professed despite his eminence, is recounted by Simplicianus in Book 8 as an example Augustine measures himself against.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pontitianus
snapshots.body: An African compatriot and imperial court official who visits Augustine and Alypius in Milan and tells them of Antony of the desert and of two officials who abandoned their careers on reading Antony's life; his story precipitates the garden crisis of Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faustus
snapshots.body: The Manichaean sect's celebrated bishop, long awaited by Augustine as the man who could resolve his doubts about Manichaean cosmology; their meeting in Carthage (Book 5) reveals Faustus as eloquent but ignorant of the sciences he was supposed to have mastered, beginning Augustine's break with the sect.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aeneas
snapshots.body: The hero of Virgil's Aeneid, whose wanderings Augustine studied and wept over as a schoolboy while remaining dry-eyed over his own spiritual death, an example of misdirected sympathy he condemns in Book 1.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dido
snapshots.body: The queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid, whose death for love Augustine was taught to weep over as a schoolboy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Creusa
snapshots.body: Aeneas's wife in Virgil's Aeneid, lost and searched for amid the fall of Troy; cited among the school poetry Augustine studied.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: The Greek epic poet, source of the school texts -- studied in the original Greek, which young Augustine hated -- that he contrasts with his ease at Latin poetry.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Virgil
snapshots.body: The Roman poet whose Aeneid supplied the school text, and the sympathetic tears over Dido, that Augustine recalls with unease in Book 1.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Terence
snapshots.body: The Roman comic playwright; Augustine cites a scene from his Eunuchus, in which a young man is incited to seduction by a painting of Jove's affair with Danae, as evidence of how pagan literature dignified vice by attaching it to the gods.

snapshots.name: Jove
snapshots.body: The chief god of the Roman pantheon, also called Jupiter. Augustine cites Terence's staging of Jove's seduction of Danae, and later a mocking list of Jove, Juno, and other gods, as examples of a religion built on stories no one would tolerate from a human being.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Danae
snapshots.body: A mythological princess visited by Jove in a shower of gold, in the story from Terence's Eunuchus that Augustine cites as pagan literature glamorizing vice by making it divine.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Juno
snapshots.body: The Roman pantheon's queen of the gods, invoked in Augustine's Book 1 catalogue of the deities his schoolboy poetry required him to praise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Venus
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of love, named among the pagan deities Augustine says his astrological and poetic education dignified without question.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Saturn
snapshots.body: A god of the Roman pantheon, listed among the planetary deities Augustine's youthful, astrology-minded studies took for granted.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mars
snapshots.body: The Roman god of war, listed among the pantheon Augustine's early education treated as unremarkable fact.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Minerva
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of wisdom and craft, named in Book 8's list of pagan deities Augustine mocks for offering no serious philosophy, only fables no better than Egypt's animal-gods.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Neptune
snapshots.body: The Roman god of the sea, named in the same mocking list of pagan deities in Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anubis
snapshots.body: The Egyptian jackal-headed god, cited by Augustine alongside the Roman pantheon as an example of gods no wiser or worthier than animals.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pylades
snapshots.body: One half of the legendary pair of devoted friends (with Orestes) each said to have been willing to die for the other, cited in Book 4 as Augustine measures his own grief and dread of death after a friend's loss.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Orestes
snapshots.body: The other half of the legendary friendship with Pylades, cited alongside him in Book 4.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Medea
snapshots.body: The sorceress of classical tragedy, invoked by way of the line "Medea flying" as an example of how even morally troubling poetry can be more honestly enjoyed than false philosophy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Catiline
snapshots.body: The Roman conspirator Lucius Sergius Catilina, cited in Book 2 as an example of evil done for its own sake rather than for any gain, a puzzle Augustine uses to examine his own boyhood theft of pears.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cicero
snapshots.body: The Roman orator and philosopher, whose dialogue Hortensius (read at nineteen) turned Augustine's ambition toward the love of wisdom itself; named later, in Books 5 and 8, as Tully.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Seneca
snapshots.body: The Roman Stoic philosopher, a few of whose books the Manichaean bishop Faustus had read -- part of the thin secular learning Augustine found beneath Faustus's famed eloquence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: The ancient Greek physician; the unnamed doctor of Book 4 cites his own early study of Hippocrates as proof he abandoned astrology only after real expertise, not ignorance.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristotle
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher. Augustine reads the Categories (which he calls "the ten Predicaments") alone and unaided at about twenty, only later realizing that a treatise he found so lucid could say nothing true about God, the one substance to which none of its categories apply.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicurus
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher of pleasure, whose creed Augustine says he would have endorsed in his more skeptical Milan years but for his belief in the soul's survival after death, which Epicurean materialism could not accommodate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adam
snapshots.body: The first man of Genesis, cited repeatedly as the origin of inherited sin and, in Book 13, in Augustine's allegorical reading of the creation narrative.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eve
snapshots.body: The first woman of Genesis, named alongside Adam in Augustine's discussions of the Fall and, in Book 13, of the allegorical Bride.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Solomon
snapshots.body: The biblical king credited with the wisdom books, quoted (unnamed as author but identified by tradition) in Augustine's warning against vain curiosity in Book 3.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Abraham
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited among the Old Testament figures whose righteousness Augustine defends against Manichaean objections, and invoked again via "Abraham's bosom" in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isaac
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited alongside Abraham and Jacob as righteous under a law suited to his own time, and again in Book 10 as an old, nearly blind man blessing his sons by inward rather than outward sight.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jacob
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited among the Old Testament righteous and, in Book 10, blessing his grandsons through Joseph despite his own blindness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Moses
snapshots.body: The lawgiver and traditional author of Genesis, cited among the Old Testament righteous in Book 3 and made the subject of sustained exegetical address in Books 11 and 12, where Augustine questions what Moses meant and intended by the creation account.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: David
snapshots.body: The biblical king and psalmist, cited among the Old Testament righteous, as the author of the Psalms sung in church (Books 9-10), and as an example of self-reproach over a small desire (his craving for water in battle, recalled in Book 10).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Esau
snapshots.body: Jacob's brother in Genesis, cited as an example of being led astray by appetite (his sale of his birthright for lentils, recalled in Book 10) and, earlier, in Augustine's discussion of divine foreknowledge and justice (Book 7).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mary
snapshots.body: The Virgin Mary, mother of Christ; Augustine recalls that his Manichaean beliefs once made him unable to accept that Christ could be born of her without being defiled by flesh.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Paul
snapshots.body: The apostle, cited repeatedly in Books 7 and 8 for his epistles on grace and the divided will, and again in Book 13's closing exegesis of his letters. Formerly named Saul, he took the name Paul, tradition held, in honor of the proconsul Paulus's conversion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Onesiphorus
snapshots.body: A disciple commended in Paul's epistles for aiding him without shame during his imprisonment, cited in Book 13's allegorical reading of Philippians on the fruits of charity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epaphroditus
snapshots.body: The Philippian messenger who carried the congregation's gift to the imprisoned Paul, named in Book 13's exegesis of Philippians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isaiah
snapshots.body: The Old Testament prophet; Ambrose recommends Augustine begin his scriptural reading with Isaiah, as the prophet who most clearly foreshadows the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Noah
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited in Book 10 as having been permitted by God to eat any kind of flesh, part of Augustine's examination of his own struggle with the pleasure of eating.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Elijah
snapshots.body: The prophet, cited twice: in Book 10, fed on flesh by God without sin, an example distinguishing lawful food from sinful appetite; in Book 13, fed by a widow who deliberately gave to a man of God, contrasted with the raven's unwitting gift, to illustrate the difference between a gift and its fruit.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tobias
snapshots.body: The blind father of the book of Tobit, cited in Book 10 as, though physically sightless, teaching his son the way of life by an inward light.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Joseph
snapshots.body: The son of Jacob in Genesis, named in Book 10 as the father of the grandsons Jacob blessed with crossed hands despite his own blindness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Manichaeus
snapshots.body: Mani, the third-century Persian founder of Manichaeism, whose own scientific claims about the heavens Augustine tested against -- and found contradicted by -- ordinary astronomical calculation, a first crack in his faith in the sect.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Helpidius
snapshots.body: A Catholic disputant at Carthage whose arguments against the Manichees, made from Scripture itself, unsettled Augustine's confidence in Manichaean answers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Symmachus
snapshots.body: Prefect of Rome, who tests and appoints Augustine to the public rhetoric chair at Milan, the position that brings him within reach of Ambrose's preaching.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vindicianus
snapshots.body: A perceptive old proconsul and former physician who tries, gently and by personal example, to talk the young Augustine out of belief in astrology.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Firminus
snapshots.body: An educated acquaintance whose precise birth-time, compared with that of a household slave born at the same hour but living a wholly different life, becomes Augustine's own decisive argument against astrology.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hierius
snapshots.body: A Roman orator Augustine never met but admired at a distance on reputation alone, cited in Book 4 as an example of the difference between being praised and being known.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Photinus
snapshots.body: A fourth-century bishop condemned as a heretic for denying Christ's divinity; Augustine recalls once holding a view of Christ close to Photinus's, as merely a man of surpassing wisdom.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cyprian
snapshots.body: The third-century bishop and martyr of Carthage; Monnica stops for a night's prayer at a seaside shrine kept in his memory, on the voyage where Augustine escapes to Rome without her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Paulus
snapshots.body: Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul converted by the apostle's preaching in Acts; Augustine repeats the tradition (of doubtful accuracy) that the apostle took the name "Paul" in honor of this convert.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julian
snapshots.body: The fourth-century Roman emperor known as Julian the Apostate; his edict barring Christians from teaching rhetoric forced Victorinus to choose between his profession and his newly professed faith, a story told by Simplicianus in Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Justina
snapshots.body: Mother of the child-emperor Valentinian and an Arian sympathizer, whose persecution of Ambrose over control of a Milan church (Book 9) the devout, including Monnica, resist by keeping vigil.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Valentinian
snapshots.body: The child Roman emperor in whose name his mother Justina presses her Arian demands against Ambrose in Milan.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gervasius
snapshots.body: One of two martyrs whose long-lost bodies Ambrose recovers by vision in Book 9, an event that includes a well-attested healing and turns public sentiment against Justina's persecution.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Protasius
snapshots.body: The second of the two martyrs discovered with Gervasius, named together with him in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euodius
snapshots.body: A young fellow-citizen of Thagaste, a former officer of the court converted and baptized before Augustine, who joins Augustine and his household on the journey back toward Africa.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Romanianus
snapshots.body: A wealthy fellow-townsman of Thagaste, considered by Augustine and his friends for the shared household of philosophical retirement they once planned, in Book 6.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Verecundus
snapshots.body: A Milanese friend, married and so unable to join the Cassiacum retreat, who lends Augustine's group his country house for it instead; he dies a Christian shortly after, a fact Augustine records with grateful relief in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antony
snapshots.body: Antony of the Desert, the Egyptian ascetic whose Life, read aloud by Pontitianus's account, drives two imperial officials to abandon their careers on the spot and becomes the story that finally breaks Augustine's resistance in the Book 8 garden scene.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Athanasius
snapshots.body: Bishop of Alexandria, remembered for having his lector recite the Psalms with so little melodic inflection that it was closer to speaking than singing -- a stricter model of church music Augustine weighs against his own delight in it (Book 10).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anaximenes
snapshots.body: The pre-Socratic philosopher who held air to be the first principle of all things; named only within Augustine's rhetorical questioning of the elements in Book 10 ("the whole air with his inhabitants answered, Anaximenes was deceived").
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Juno
snapshots.body: The Roman pantheon's queen of the gods, invoked in Augustine's Book 1 catalogue of the deities his schoolboy poetry required him to praise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Venus
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of love, named among the pagan deities Augustine says his astrological and poetic education dignified without question.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Saturn
snapshots.body: A god of the Roman pantheon, listed among the planetary deities Augustine's youthful, astrology-minded studies took for granted.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mars
snapshots.body: The Roman god of war, listed among the pantheon Augustine's early education treated as unremarkable fact.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Minerva
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of wisdom and craft, named in Book 8's list of pagan deities Augustine mocks for offering no serious philosophy, only fables no better than Egypt's animal-gods.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Neptune
snapshots.body: The Roman god of the sea, named in the same mocking list of pagan deities in Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anubis
snapshots.body: The Egyptian jackal-headed god, cited by Augustine alongside the Roman pantheon as an example of gods no wiser or worthier than animals.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pylades
snapshots.body: One half of the legendary pair of devoted friends (with Orestes) each said to have been willing to die for the other, cited in Book 4 as Augustine measures his own grief and dread of death after a friend's loss.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Orestes
snapshots.body: The other half of the legendary friendship with Pylades, cited alongside him in Book 4.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Medea
snapshots.body: The sorceress of classical tragedy, invoked by way of the line "Medea flying" as an example of how even morally troubling poetry can be more honestly enjoyed than false philosophy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Catiline
snapshots.body: The Roman conspirator Lucius Sergius Catilina, cited in Book 2 as an example of evil done for its own sake rather than for any gain, a puzzle Augustine uses to examine his own boyhood theft of pears.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cicero
snapshots.body: The Roman orator and philosopher, whose dialogue Hortensius (read at nineteen) turned Augustine's ambition toward the love of wisdom itself; named later, in Books 5 and 8, as Tully.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Seneca
snapshots.body: The Roman Stoic philosopher, a few of whose books the Manichaean bishop Faustus had read -- part of the thin secular learning Augustine found beneath Faustus's famed eloquence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: The ancient Greek physician; the unnamed doctor of Book 4 cites his own early study of Hippocrates as proof he abandoned astrology only after real expertise, not ignorance.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristotle
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher. Augustine reads the Categories (which he calls "the ten Predicaments") alone and unaided at about twenty, only later realizing that a treatise he found so lucid could say nothing true about God, the one substance to which none of its categories apply.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicurus
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher of pleasure, whose creed Augustine says he would have endorsed in his more skeptical Milan years but for his belief in the soul's survival after death, which Epicurean materialism could not accommodate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adam
snapshots.body: The first man of Genesis, cited repeatedly as the origin of inherited sin and, in Book 13, in Augustine's allegorical reading of the creation narrative.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eve
snapshots.body: The first woman of Genesis, named alongside Adam in Augustine's discussions of the Fall and, in Book 13, of the allegorical Bride.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Solomon
snapshots.body: The biblical king credited with the wisdom books, quoted (unnamed as author but identified by tradition) in Augustine's warning against vain curiosity in Book 3.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Abraham
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited among the Old Testament figures whose righteousness Augustine defends against Manichaean objections, and invoked again via "Abraham's bosom" in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isaac
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited alongside Abraham and Jacob as righteous under a law suited to his own time, and again in Book 10 as an old, nearly blind man blessing his sons by inward rather than outward sight.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jacob
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited among the Old Testament righteous and, in Book 10, blessing his grandsons through Joseph despite his own blindness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Moses
snapshots.body: The lawgiver and traditional author of Genesis, cited among the Old Testament righteous in Book 3 and made the subject of sustained exegetical address in Books 11 and 12, where Augustine questions what Moses meant and intended by the creation account.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: David
snapshots.body: The biblical king and psalmist, cited among the Old Testament righteous, as the author of the Psalms sung in church (Books 9-10), and as an example of self-reproach over a small desire (his craving for water in battle, recalled in Book 10).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Esau
snapshots.body: Jacob's brother in Genesis, cited as an example of being led astray by appetite (his sale of his birthright for lentils, recalled in Book 10) and, earlier, in Augustine's discussion of divine foreknowledge and justice (Book 7).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mary
snapshots.body: The Virgin Mary, mother of Christ; Augustine recalls that his Manichaean beliefs once made him unable to accept that Christ could be born of her without being defiled by flesh.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Paul
snapshots.body: The apostle, cited repeatedly in Books 7 and 8 for his epistles on grace and the divided will, and again in Book 13's closing exegesis of his letters. Formerly named Saul, he took the name Paul, tradition held, in honor of the proconsul Paulus's conversion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Onesiphorus
snapshots.body: A disciple commended in Paul's epistles for aiding him without shame during his imprisonment, cited in Book 13's allegorical reading of Philippians on the fruits of charity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epaphroditus
snapshots.body: The Philippian messenger who carried the congregation's gift to the imprisoned Paul, named in Book 13's exegesis of Philippians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isaiah
snapshots.body: The Old Testament prophet; Ambrose recommends Augustine begin his scriptural reading with Isaiah, as the prophet who most clearly foreshadows the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Noah
snapshots.body: The patriarch of Genesis, cited in Book 10 as having been permitted by God to eat any kind of flesh, part of Augustine's examination of his own struggle with the pleasure of eating.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Elijah
snapshots.body: The prophet, cited twice: in Book 10, fed on flesh by God without sin, an example distinguishing lawful food from sinful appetite; in Book 13, fed by a widow who deliberately gave to a man of God, contrasted with the raven's unwitting gift, to illustrate the difference between a gift and its fruit.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tobias
snapshots.body: The blind father of the book of Tobit, cited in Book 10 as, though physically sightless, teaching his son the way of life by an inward light.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Joseph
snapshots.body: The son of Jacob in Genesis, named in Book 10 as the father of the grandsons Jacob blessed with crossed hands despite his own blindness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Manichaeus
snapshots.body: Mani, the third-century Persian founder of Manichaeism, whose own scientific claims about the heavens Augustine tested against -- and found contradicted by -- ordinary astronomical calculation, a first crack in his faith in the sect.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Helpidius
snapshots.body: A Catholic disputant at Carthage whose arguments against the Manichees, made from Scripture itself, unsettled Augustine's confidence in Manichaean answers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Symmachus
snapshots.body: Prefect of Rome, who tests and appoints Augustine to the public rhetoric chair at Milan, the position that brings him within reach of Ambrose's preaching.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vindicianus
snapshots.body: A perceptive old proconsul and former physician who tries, gently and by personal example, to talk the young Augustine out of belief in astrology.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Firminus
snapshots.body: An educated acquaintance whose precise birth-time, compared with that of a household slave born at the same hour but living a wholly different life, becomes Augustine's own decisive argument against astrology.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hierius
snapshots.body: A Roman orator Augustine never met but admired at a distance on reputation alone, cited in Book 4 as an example of the difference between being praised and being known.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Photinus
snapshots.body: A fourth-century bishop condemned as a heretic for denying Christ's divinity; Augustine recalls once holding a view of Christ close to Photinus's, as merely a man of surpassing wisdom.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cyprian
snapshots.body: The third-century bishop and martyr of Carthage; Monnica stops for a night's prayer at a seaside shrine kept in his memory, on the voyage where Augustine escapes to Rome without her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Paulus
snapshots.body: Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul converted by the apostle's preaching in Acts; Augustine repeats the tradition (of doubtful accuracy) that the apostle took the name "Paul" in honor of this convert.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julian
snapshots.body: The fourth-century Roman emperor known as Julian the Apostate; his edict barring Christians from teaching rhetoric forced Victorinus to choose between his profession and his newly professed faith, a story told by Simplicianus in Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Justina
snapshots.body: Mother of the child-emperor Valentinian and an Arian sympathizer, whose persecution of Ambrose over control of a Milan church (Book 9) the devout, including Monnica, resist by keeping vigil.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Valentinian
snapshots.body: The child Roman emperor in whose name his mother Justina presses her Arian demands against Ambrose in Milan.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gervasius
snapshots.body: One of two martyrs whose long-lost bodies Ambrose recovers by vision in Book 9, an event that includes a well-attested healing and turns public sentiment against Justina's persecution.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Protasius
snapshots.body: The second of the two martyrs discovered with Gervasius, named together with him in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euodius
snapshots.body: A young fellow-citizen of Thagaste, a former officer of the court converted and baptized before Augustine, who joins Augustine and his household on the journey back toward Africa.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Romanianus
snapshots.body: A wealthy fellow-townsman of Thagaste, considered by Augustine and his friends for the shared household of philosophical retirement they once planned, in Book 6.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Verecundus
snapshots.body: A Milanese friend, married and so unable to join the Cassiacum retreat, who lends Augustine's group his country house for it instead; he dies a Christian shortly after, a fact Augustine records with grateful relief in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antony
snapshots.body: Antony of the Desert, the Egyptian ascetic whose Life, read aloud by Pontitianus's account, drives two imperial officials to abandon their careers on the spot and becomes the story that finally breaks Augustine's resistance in the Book 8 garden scene.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Athanasius
snapshots.body: Bishop of Alexandria, remembered for having his lector recite the Psalms with so little melodic inflection that it was closer to speaking than singing -- a stricter model of church music Augustine weighs against his own delight in it (Book 10).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anaximenes
snapshots.body: The pre-Socratic philosopher who held air to be the first principle of all things; named only within Augustine's rhetorical questioning of the elements in Book 10 ("the whole air with his inhabitants answered, Anaximenes was deceived").
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.
